scope: Two-sided entropy bounds for the Hermitian zero-reference normalization dual, its finite domain, and shorter exposition of the general-measure research questions.

edits.new:
\section{Entropy bounds in a Hermitian background}

For a Hermitian background and reference zero, the dual functional need not equal entropy plus a constant. Its finite domain is nevertheless the finite-entropy domain.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:hermitian-dual-entropy-bounds}
Let $\theta=\omega$ be Hermitian, let $\varphi=0$, and normalize $\mathrm{d}V(X)=1$. For every $q>1$ there is a finite real constant $a_q$, and there is a finite real constant $A$, such that every Borel probability measure $\nu$ satisfies
\[
 a_q+\frac1q\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(\nu)
 \leq H_0(\nu)
 \leq A+n\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(\nu).
\]
The inequalities include the value $+\infty$. Thus $H_0(\nu)<\infty$ if and only if $\nu$ has finite entropy. A family of probabilities has uniformly bounded $H_0$ if and only if its entropies are uniformly bounded. Neither mass property is assumed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In dimension one the closed formula \eqref{eq:normalization-closed-formula} gives $H_0=\log\int_X\omega+\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}$, so the assertions follow. Suppose $n\geq2$.

For $G\in C(X)$, apply \cref{thm:lp-potential-estimate} to a bounded solution with density $\mathrm{e}^{B_0(G)+G}$. It gives a constant $c_q>0$, independent of $G$, such that
\[
 B_0(G)\geq\log c_q-\frac1q\log\int_X\mathrm{e}^{qG}\,\mathrm{d}V.
\]
For the other bound, fix a smooth Gauduchon metric $\gamma$, rescaled so that $\int_X\omega\wedge\gamma^{n-1}=1$, and write
\[
 k_\gamma=\left(\frac{\gamma^n}{\mathrm{d}V}\right)^{(n-1)/n},
 \qquad m=\min_X k_\gamma>0.
\]
For smooth $G$, the smooth equation, matrix arithmetic--geometric mean and Stokes give
\[
 \mathrm{e}^{B_0(G)/n}\int_X\mathrm{e}^{G/n}k_\gamma\,\mathrm{d}V\leq1.
\]
Uniform approximation and continuity of $B_0$ extend this inequality to continuous $G$. Consequently
\[
 B_0(G)\leq-n\log m-n\log\int_X\mathrm{e}^{G/n}\,\mathrm{d}V.
\]

For an absolutely continuous probability $\nu$, the variational calculation in the proof of \cref{prop:normalization-dual-entropy} gives
\[
 \sup_{F\in C(X)}\left(\int_XF\,\mathrm{d}\nu
                 -\log\int_X\mathrm{e}^F\,\mathrm{d}V\right)
       =\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(\nu),
\]
including infinite entropy. This measure-theoretic identity requires no closedness. Taking suprema in the two bounds for $B_0$, with $F=qG$ and $F=G/n$, proves the claim with $a_q=\log c_q$ and $A=-n\log m$.

\Needspace{4\baselineskip}
For every other probability, both $H_0$ and entropy are infinite by \cref{thm:normalization-dual-compactness}. Fix $q=2$ for the assertions about finite domains and uniformly bounded families.
\end{proof}

In particular the compact dual sublevels of \cref{thm:normalization-dual-compactness} have uniformly bounded entropy in this Hermitian zero-reference regime. This does not identify $H_0$ with entropy, bound the probability densities in a fixed $L^p$ space, or extend the assertion to an arbitrary singular reference.

edits.old: The general non-pluripolar measure theorem in \cref{thm:als-general-measure} is a result of \cite{ALS26}. Its complete proof is reconstructed in \cref{sec:general-measure-relative}, with $\theta$ semipositive and big, the displayed model condition, and $v_-(\theta)>0$. Bounded mass is not assumed. Both the positive-exponent equation and the zero-exponent equation with its unique positive scalar are covered.
edits.new: Two general-measure regimes have been reconstructed. For a semipositive big background, \cref{sec:general-measure-relative} proves \cref{thm:als-general-measure} of \cite{ALS26}, with its model condition and $v_-(\theta)>0$, without bounded mass. It covers the positive-exponent equation and the zero-exponent equation with its unique positive scalar. For an arbitrary smooth big background, \cref{thm:big-model-exponential,thm:big-model-normalized} proves both equations under bounded mass and positive lower volume of the model reference. The latter hypothesis implies metric positive lower volume in this regime, as explained after \cref{thm:li-general-measure}. \Cref{cor:big-model-lp-type} gives the prescribed ordinary type for $L^p$ densities, whereas the minimal ordinary-type $L^p$ theorem in \cref{sec:big-minimal-existence} needs neither metric volume property.

edits.old: The key capacity argument uses relative zero-domination without assuming that the limiting lower roof has finite mass. Its proof first constructs an auxiliary envelope whose measure is carried where that envelope is nonnegative. Locality with one bounded truncation proves finiteness of this auxiliary measure, so the earlier finite-measure domination theorem applies without circularity. Contact support, weighted lower semicontinuity under capacity convergence, and the common exponential envelope then give the moving-measure limit. Uniform sublevel tails prove finiteness of the equation's limiting measure afterwards.
edits.new: The two proofs use different compactness estimates. In the semipositive argument, relative zero-domination constructs an auxiliary envelope whose measure is supported where the envelope is nonnegative. Locality with one bounded truncation proves that this auxiliary measure is finite; the limiting lower roof need not have finite mass. Contact support, weighted lower semicontinuity under capacity convergence and a common exponential envelope give the moving-measure limit. Uniform sublevel tails then prove finiteness of the solution measure. The arbitrary-background argument uses an explicit rooftop between different classes and finite upper relative volumes for compactness and weighted-mass maximization. Removing bounded mass requires replacing these estimates and still proving finiteness of the solution measure; existence of the formal envelopes alone is insufficient.

edits.old: For arbitrary smooth big backgrounds, \cref{thm:big-model-exponential,thm:big-model-normalized} prove both equations under bounded mass and positive lower volume of the model reference. The relative projection is built from an explicit rooftop between different classes. Weighted-mass maximization then gives existence, and \cref{cor:big-model-lp-type} proves ordinary singularity type for $L^p$ data. Metric positive lower volume is automatic under these hypotheses, by the comparison following \cref{thm:li-general-measure}. The earlier minimal ordinary-type $L^p$ theorem in \cref{sec:big-minimal-existence} needs neither metric volume property.
edits.new: Universal solvability cannot omit the lower-volume condition. In a Hermitian background, \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-solvability} characterizes solvability for every finite non-pluripolar measure by $v_-(h)>0$. When it vanishes, \cref{thm:lower-mass-obstructing-measure} gives an $L^1$ probability density, bounded below by a positive constant, which admits no positive scaled subsolution among genuine potentials. These obstructing densities are $L^1$ dense, although every smooth strictly positive density is solvable. \Cref{thm:vanishing-lower-mass} realizes this obstruction on a compact threefold.

edits.old:
The lower-volume assumption cannot simply be omitted from a theorem for all non-pluripolar measures. For a Hermitian background, \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-solvability} characterizes that universal solvability by $v_-(h)>0$. If it vanishes, \cref{thm:lower-mass-obstructing-measure} constructs an $L^1$ probability density, bounded below by a positive constant, with no positive scaled subsolution even among arbitrary genuine potentials. Such obstructing densities are $L^1$ dense, whereas every smooth strictly positive density is solvable. The geometric example in \cref{thm:vanishing-lower-mass} makes this obstruction concrete.

For an individual nonnegative $L^1$ density, \cref{thm:individual-density-subsolution} gives an attained subsolution threshold: the decreasing limit $b_h(f)$ of the bounded-truncation normalization constants is positive exactly when some positive multiple of $f\,\mathrm{d}V$ is dominated by an extended Monge--Amp\`ere measure. The construction uses upper envelopes and damped continuity; it does not identify an exact equation or a finite-mass singularity class. Smooth tests alone do not suffice, by \cref{thm:smooth-tests-insufficient}. The exact Gauduchon formula in \cref{thm:integrable-gauduchon-formula} makes the threshold upper semicontinuous in $L^1$. It also describes a Banach space of admissible density roots, independent of the Hermitian metric, in \cref{prop:individual-density-banach,prop:individual-threshold-backgrounds}. Positive lower mass makes its domain all of $L^n$; finite upper mass makes its root norm complete. These are separate properties, as proved in \cref{prop:individual-root-completeness}.
edits.new: For an individual nonnegative $L^1$ density, the relevant number is the attained subsolution threshold $b_h(f)$ of \cref{thm:individual-density-subsolution}. It is the decreasing limit of the bounded-truncation normalization constants and is positive exactly when some positive multiple of $f\,\mathrm{d}V$ is dominated by an extended Monge--Amp\`ere measure. The upper-envelope and damped-continuity proof gives a subsolution, without asserting an exact equation or finite mass. Smooth tests alone do not suffice, by \cref{thm:smooth-tests-insufficient}. The Gauduchon formula in \cref{thm:integrable-gauduchon-formula} makes the threshold upper semicontinuous in $L^1$ and identifies the Banach space of admissible density roots. This space is independent of the Hermitian metric by \cref{prop:individual-density-banach,prop:individual-threshold-backgrounds}. Positive lower mass makes its domain all of $L^n$; finite upper mass makes the root norm complete, by \cref{prop:individual-root-completeness}. These are distinct properties.

edits.old: Under $v_-(h)>0$, \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-exact-threshold} gives an exact solution in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ for every nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ density. Its proof identifies the scalar by finite-measure comparison, and dominated continuity gives capacity convergence along every $L^1$-convergent subsequence of the normalized greatest exponential solutions. This includes the Hopf example without bounded mass. For $L^p$ densities, $p>1$, the continuous equation and \cref{prop:individual-normalizer-lp} give the answer without positive lower mass.
edits.new: There are two established general cases. Under $v_-(h)>0$, \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-exact-threshold} gives an exact solution in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ for every nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ density. Finite-measure comparison identifies its scalar, and dominated continuity gives capacity convergence along every $L^1$-convergent subsequence of normalized greatest exponential solutions. This includes the Hopf example without bounded mass. For $L^p$ densities, $p>1$, the continuous equation and \cref{prop:individual-normalizer-lp} give the answer without positive lower mass.

edits.old: The remaining case in \cref{qu:individual-equation-threshold} has $v_-(h)=0$ and a positive individual threshold. In this regime \cref{cor:individual-positive-threshold-exponential} gives the greatest exponential solutions and the scalar and total-variation limits, but capacity convergence of their normalized potentials still needs proof. Under the root-tail condition, \cref{prop:exponential-root-tail-modulus} quantifies the scalar and total-variation errors. Its modulus tends to zero; a bound linear in the exponent requires additional control. Positivity and integrability of the density alone do not guarantee a positive threshold. When $b_h(f)=0$, existence of an exponential subsolution is a separate question. Arbitrary non-pluripolar measures also require an extension of the density criterion.
edits.new: The remaining case in \cref{qu:individual-equation-threshold} has $v_-(h)=0$ and $b_h(f)>0$. \Cref{cor:individual-positive-threshold-exponential} gives greatest exponential solutions, convergence of their scalars to $b_h(f)$ and total-variation convergence of their measures. Capacity convergence of the normalized potentials is the missing step. Under the root-tail condition of \cref{prop:root-uniform-tails}, \cref{prop:exponential-root-tail-modulus} quantifies the scalar and measure errors; a rate linear in the exponent needs additional control. Positivity and integrability of $f$ alone do not ensure a positive threshold. Exponential subsolutions when $b_h(f)=0$, and an extension of the density criterion to arbitrary non-pluripolar measures, are separate questions.

edits.old: The uniform tail criterion in \cref{prop:root-uniform-tails} identifies the closure $\mathcal D_h^0$ of bounded roots. For densities with roots in this space, \cref{thm:integrable-current-attainment,prop:integrable-threshold-adjoints} give an attained compact Gauduchon dual problem and absolutely continuous supporting probabilities. The trace errors along smooth maximizing sequences tend to zero in total variation by \cref{prop:threshold-trace-saturation}.
edits.new: Gauduchon dual attainment gives several sufficient regimes. If the density root lies in the bounded-root closure $\mathcal D_h^0$, \cref{thm:integrable-current-attainment,prop:integrable-threshold-adjoints} give a maximizing current and represent all supporting probabilities. These probabilities are absolutely continuous, and the trace errors along smooth maximizing sequences tend to zero in total variation by \cref{prop:threshold-trace-saturation}. Uniform integrability along just one maximizing sequence already gives a maximizing current and convergence of its determinant-weighted measures, by \cref{prop:selected-gauduchon-attainment}. This weaker hypothesis on the chosen sequence does not establish the representation of all supporting probabilities.

edits.old: In dimension at least two, a smooth strictly positive maximizer forces every threshold subsolution to be smooth and exact, and the density root to have a smooth nonnegative representative, by \cref{cor:smooth-dual-exact-equation}. The solution is unique modulo constants. For a closed background, \cref{cor:kahler-smooth-dual-attainment} characterizes smooth dual attainment by smooth strict positivity of the density. This last positivity conclusion fails for nonclosed backgrounds, as \cref{ex:nonclosed-dual-zero-density} shows on every compact complex manifold of dimension at least two.
edits.new: In dimension at least two, a smooth strictly positive maximizer forces every threshold subsolution to be smooth and exact, with uniqueness modulo constants, and makes the density root smooth and nonnegative; see \cref{cor:smooth-dual-exact-equation}. For a closed background, \cref{cor:kahler-smooth-dual-attainment} characterizes smooth dual attainment by smooth strict positivity of the density. The strict positivity conclusion fails for nonclosed backgrounds on every compact complex manifold of dimension at least two, by \cref{ex:nonclosed-dual-zero-density}.

edits.old: At a positive threshold and in dimension at least two, \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} allows a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives the exact global equation, smoothness off $Z$, and uniqueness of all threshold subsolutions modulo constants. The uniqueness proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to remove the resulting nonpositive divisorial difference. It requires no prescribed singularity type. The classes of the positive pole divisors are then linearly independent by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-divisor-independence}.
edits.new: \Cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} also allows a smooth semipositive maximizer which is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives an exact global equation, smoothness off $Z$ and uniqueness of all threshold subsolutions modulo constants. The proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to eliminate their divisorial difference; no singularity type is prescribed. The positive pole-divisor classes are linearly independent by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-divisor-independence}. In this regime \cref{prop:semipositive-dual-exponential-limit} gives whole-family normalized $L^1$ convergence, a fixed lower barrier and $b\leq c_\lambda\leq b\mathrm{e}^{C\lambda}$. A genuine smaller-background envelope of the threshold solution gives capacity convergence by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-capacity-limit}; $L^p$ data with $p>1$ give a continuous solution and uniform convergence by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-lp-limit}. \Cref{ex:semipositive-projective-maximizer} has a smooth solution but a nondifferentiable density root on $Z$. For general $L^1$ data, automatic genuineness of that envelope and regularity across $Z$ remain open here.

edits.old: \Cref{prop:semipositive-dual-exponential-limit} proves whole-family normalized $L^1$ convergence of the exponential solutions, with a fixed lower barrier and $b\leq c_\lambda\leq b\mathrm{e}^{C\lambda}$. If the threshold solution also admits a genuine smaller-background envelope, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-capacity-limit} strengthens this to capacity convergence. For $f\in L^p$, $p>1$, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-lp-limit} gives a continuous threshold solution and whole-family uniform convergence. The branched projective example in \cref{ex:semipositive-projective-maximizer} has a smooth threshold solution but a nondifferentiable density root along $Z$. For general $L^1$ data, automatic genuineness of the smaller-background envelope and global regularity across $Z$ remain open here.
edits.new: The moment criterion \cref{thm:gauduchon-moment-threshold} uses no regularity of a maximizing current. Uniform first moments of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions against one smooth maximizing sequence give a fixed lower barrier for the exponential solutions. Their normalized cluster limits lie below the greatest normalized threshold subsolution $\Phi_f$. If $P_{\delta h}(\Phi_f)$ is genuine for some $0<\delta<1$, the lower-barrier criterion gives subsequential capacity convergence and an exact threshold equation, without either mass property. An entropy bound on the test probabilities supplies both the first moments and the selected-sequence uniform integrability above. By \cref{prop:hermitian-dual-entropy-bounds}, such an entropy bound is equivalent to a uniform bound for the Hermitian zero-reference dual $H_0$ on these probabilities. It supplies no smaller-background envelope.

edits.old: A different sufficient condition is \cref{thm:gauduchon-moment-threshold}. Uniform first moments of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions against one smooth maximizing sequence give a fixed lower barrier for the exponential solutions. The greatest normalized threshold subsolution $\Phi_f$ bounds every cluster limit from above. If $P_{\delta h}(\Phi_f)$ is genuine for some $0<\delta<1$, the lower-barrier criterion then gives subsequential capacity convergence and an exact threshold equation, without either mass property. This does not require a regular maximizing current. The moment bound and smaller-background envelope remain additional assumptions.
edits.new: Thus singular-current attainment alone does not settle the equation. At zero lower mass, it is still unknown here whether root tails suffice, or even whether $\mathcal D_h^0=\mathcal D_h$. \Cref{prop:root-tail-continuity} characterizes the tail condition by continuity under uniformly bounded logarithmic perturbations tending to zero in measure. This is an order-interval statement, not unrestricted $L^1$ continuity of the threshold.

edits.old:
Uniform integrability along one maximizing sequence already gives a maximizing current and convergence of its determinant-weighted measures, by \cref{prop:selected-gauduchon-attainment}. An entropy bound on the corresponding probabilities supplies both this uniform integrability and the first-moment bound. It does not supply the smaller-background envelope. Attainment by a singular current does not supply either regularity argument. When lower mass vanishes, whether the root-tail condition suffices for the exact equation in \cref{qu:individual-equation-threshold} remains to be determined. When $v_-(h)=0$, even equality $\mathcal D_h^0=\mathcal D_h$ is not established here. The approximation condition is characterized by continuity under uniformly bounded logarithmic perturbations tending to zero in measure in \cref{prop:root-tail-continuity}; it is not unrestricted $L^1$ continuity of the density threshold.

The next extension concerns arbitrary big backgrounds without bounded mass. The semipositive construction uses a smaller-background reference and an auxiliary finite measure; the arbitrary-background construction instead uses finite upper relative volumes for its rooftop and compactness arguments. A general extension must replace those particular uses, and must still prove that the solution measure is finite. Existence of all the formal envelopes, without the required measure estimates, would not suffice.

The distinction between an envelope class and a finite-mass class remains necessary. The prescribed-type carrier in \cref{prop:relative-measure-carrier} can be unbounded and have infinite extended mass, so its representation does not directly invoke the bounded subsolution theorem. In the semipositive prescribed-reference proof, the comparison potential is instead obtained from the already proved minimal-reference equation and compared using reference zero.

Nor does the completed argument restore unrestricted $L^1$ continuity of the operator. The finite atomic curve models in \cref{thm:curve-ideal-lone-completion} converge to a smooth positive-mass potential while their non-pluripolar measures vanish. The Monge--Amp\`ere measure of a maximum can also acquire mass on its interface. The proof therefore derives capacity convergence from its specific measure control and uses contact pieces of lower envelopes, with the exact inequalities proved earlier.
edits.new: Two cautions about the existence proofs remain essential. The prescribed-type carrier of \cref{prop:relative-measure-carrier} can be unbounded and have infinite extended mass, so it cannot directly invoke the bounded subsolution theorem. The semipositive proof instead obtains its comparison potential from the minimal-reference equation and compares it using reference zero. Nor can an $L^1$ limit be inserted directly into a Monge--Amp\`ere equation: the finite atomic curve models of \cref{thm:curve-ideal-lone-completion} converge to a smooth positive-mass potential while their non-pluripolar measures vanish, and the measure of a maximum can acquire interface mass. The existence proofs therefore derive capacity convergence from their specific measure control and use the proved contact inequalities on the appropriate pieces of lower envelopes.
